PMGT1852 Week 11

PMGT1852 Week 11 - The Secrets to Capturing the Record: The Power of the Pen

Overview

The facilitator holds the pen, and with it the power to shape what the meeting decides. This week covers:

• Five common abuses of the power of the pen.

• The four rules for using the pen properly: write first, discuss second; write what they said; write so they can read it; ask, do not tell.

• What to capture: decisions, actions, outstanding issues, relevant analysis and comments.

• The structure of a sample meeting document.

• Keeping the record concise with noun-verb-object phrasing and the headline technique.

• Avoiding lulls (dead air) while writing.

Key Concepts

Power of the pen

Power of the pen is the influence that comes from controlling what gets written down during a facilitated session. The secret for using it well is to learn from how others abuse it.

The official record

What is written down is the meeting's official record. Participants must know this, and the facilitator must gain their agreement to it at the start of the meeting.

Headline technique

The headline technique shortens a long comment into a headline-style statement that keeps the meaning but drops the extra words.

Frameworks and Formulas

Five common abuses of the pen

The facilitator decides for themselves which comments are worth capturing.

Asking the group's permission before writing down what someone said.

Writing the facilitator's own interpretation instead of the speaker's words.

Asking permission to use the facilitator's own wording instead of the speaker's.

Waiting until a comment is "perfect" before writing it down.

Four rules: using, not abusing, the pen

Rule

What it means

Write first, discuss second

Incomplete, improvable, not the answer you wanted, even plainly wrong - write it down anyway. The record holds their words, not yours; your opinion must not filter it; writing immediately avoids slowing the pace with "Sorry, what did you say again?"; and it keeps the facilitator on track

Write what they said, not what you heard

Rewording people's comments implies "you cannot say it well, I will say it for you". Over time less forceful participants wait for you to polish their words, forceful ones argue over wording, and because the words are not theirs, ownership of the result drops. This rule is essential for empowering participants

Write so the group can read it

Large letters (about 10 lines per flip-chart page); write straight and leave room for changes; dark colours for the original text, lighter colours for additions and edits; title every page

Ask, do not tell

If you tell instead of asking, participants may agree without owning the idea, may disagree and cost time in persuasion, and may see you as taking sides - destroying your credibility as a neutral facilitator

What to capture

Decisions made.

Actions assigned.

Outstanding issues.

Relevant analysis and comments.

Keeping the record concise (four methods)

Give people an answer template, for example noun-verb-object ("HR places ad", "PM schedules meetings").

Capture only as many words as the comment needs to be clear and to stand on its own (for example: "In project phase, PM calls for fortnightly status meetings").

Use common abbreviations.

Shorten long comments with the headline technique.

Worked Examples

The structure of a sample meeting document

• Part I - the meeting itself: a title (team name), date, time and place of the meeting, the list of attendees, who chaired and who took the notes, a one-sentence statement of purpose, the team goal, and the complete agenda (for example items A to G: getting started, current process, problems, potential improvements, prioritise, implementation plan, review and close), with a note of which items were discussed (for example A to C). Information the facilitator adds for clarity or context is shown in italics, so readers can tell it apart from what was said in the room.

• Part II - the participants' words: the facilitator's capture of what participants actually said on important topics, including a concise list of the current process steps (eight steps in the worked example).

• Part III - the outputs: the problems list, the next steps (the date and time of the next meeting), a dated Decisions list, and an Actions list with three columns - action, person and deadline. All of these come from the parking boards. A completed action appears once as "done" in the next meeting's document and is then removed.

Avoiding lulls while writing

Different participants react differently to the silence while the facilitator writes: patient ones wait; impatient ones (often the majority) answer the next question before you are ready; talkative ones start private conversations; forceful ones show impatience, do something else, or make negative comments.

Ways to reduce lulls - have participants fill the gap while you write:

• Repeat the words as you write them, then probe: "to do what?" and "Why is that important?".

• Stand near the flip chart or whiteboard.

• Start writing as soon as you hear the first capturable word.

• Ask the speaker to repeat part of the comment.

• Ask a direct follow-up question (a probe).

• Use a scribe who understands the power of the pen.

Worked dialogue: while writing "Utilize online directories ...", the facilitator repeats the phrase, asks "to do what?", and then "Why is that important?" - the speaker keeps talking and the silence disappears.
